title: So You Need a Sponsor — A Practical Guide for Tier 1 and Tier 2 Citizens Pursuing Tier Advancement
body:
So You Need a Sponsor
A Practical Guide for Tier 1 and Tier 2 Citizens Pursuing Tier Advancement

Published by the Gray Zone Community Advocacy Collective | Third Edition | Circulated freely
This document is not affiliated with the GLMZ Citizen Benefits Bureau.

---

LET'S START WITH WHAT IT IS

You've read Article 7.3. Or someone read it to you, or you heard about it secondhand. The Bureau document is sixty-nine paragraphs of administrative language designed to describe something simple in a way that sounds like policy rather than what it is.

What it is: to move up a Tier, you need someone from two Tiers above you to sign a document saying you deserve it, watch you for three years, and pay a surety bond if you fail. They volunteer to do this. The Bureau doesn't pay them. There is no formal system for finding them.

You have to ask.

---

WHO WILL SAY YES

The honest answer is that very few people will say yes. We're telling you this upfront because going in with accurate expectations is better than going in with hope that gets destroyed.

A Tier 4 Citizen taking on a Tier 2 petition assumes:
  — Six months of financial surety (typically Φ 3,000–12,000 depending on the benefits increase)
  — Three years of quarterly paperwork
  — Personal and legal exposure if you violate conduct rules
  — The social perception, among their own peers, of being someone who sponsors people from the Gray Zone

That last point matters more than the money. Being a known Sponsor is not prestigious among Tier 4 and 5 peers. It reads as either naive idealism or as something morally suspicious — as though the Sponsor wants something from the arrangement. There are people who want things. We discuss this below.

The people most likely to say yes:

  1. Employers with a direct interest in your productivity. If a Tier 4 employer needs you doing Tier 3 work without the overhead of a Tier 3 contract, Tier advancement is cheap for them and expensive for you. Ask about this carefully.

  2. Activists and advocates. They exist. They are rarer than they were before the 2218 revisions increased the surety requirement. The advocacy groups that facilitate genuine sponsorships are listed at the end of this document.

  3. Family. If you have a family member who has advanced, they may be eligible to sponsor you. This is the least complicated Sponsorship relationship but it is emotionally complicated in ways we don't need to explain.

  4. Religious and community organizations with Tier 4 leadership. Some do this. Some charge for it in ways the Bureau cannot see. Ask directly what is expected of you.

---

WHAT THEY WILL ASK FOR

The Bureau protocol says Sponsorship is voluntary and civic. This is accurate and meaningless. People who spend their personal money and legal exposure on strangers do so for reasons.

Reasonable asks: references from your employer, work history, documentation of your conduct record, a written statement of your goals, regular check-ins.

Red flags: requests for labor ('I just need some help around the property'), requests for money, requests that occur in private settings without documentation, requests that involve any conduct that makes you uncomfortable. These are not legal under Article 12.1. They happen. Keep records.

The power imbalance in a Sponsorship relationship is structural. Your Sponsor can withdraw at any time (subject to surety return, but they can withdraw). You cannot exit the relationship without it affecting your advancement. This is the design of the system.

---

HOW TO APPROACH A POTENTIAL SPONSOR

With documentation. Bring:
  — Your current Tier certification
  — Your conduct record (available from your district Tier Management Office; Tier 2 walk-in service is available Tuesdays and Thursdays, 9-12)
  — Your employment history
  — A brief written summary of why you are seeking advancement and what you intend to do with improved Citizen Benefits

With patience. Most first approaches fail. This is not a reflection of your worth. It is a reflection of the structural disincentives.

With your eyes open. Read Article 7.3.4 carefully. The Bureau explicitly notes that it does not regulate the personal relationship between you and your Sponsor. This is not a protection. This is an absence of protection. Plan accordingly.

---

A NOTE ON SPONSORSHIP VIOLENCE

The Bureau classifies violence against Sponsors as a Tier Protocol Violation. We are not going to pretend this doesn't happen, because pretending it doesn't happen is how the Bureau uses it.

When a Tier 1 or Tier 2 Citizen assaults or kills their Sponsor, the Bureau counts it in the Tier System Integrity Report and uses the count to argue that lower-tier Citizens require more monitoring, less access, and harder advancement criteria. The 2218 revision — the one that increased your surety requirement and added two years to the Sponsorship Period — was justified partly by citing a twenty-three-incident spike in Sponsorship Violence in 2216-2217.

The Bureau does not count, in any public document, the number of lower-tier Citizens who report coercion, exploitation, or abuse by Sponsors. That number is not compiled. There is no report.

The violence happens. It happens because the Sponsorship system creates conditions of profound dependency and then provides no institutional protection for the dependent party. People in impossible positions do things that are impossible to defend. The Bureau records the outcome and calls it evidence of their nature.

---

COMMUNITY SPONSORSHIP RESOURCES

The following organizations have been verified by the Gray Zone Community Advocacy Collective to provide legitimate, non-exploitative sponsorship facilitation. This list is updated quarterly. If an organization is not on this list, that does not mean it is illegitimate. Ask questions.

  — The Meridian Compact Advocacy Office, District 7 (Tuesdays, community center, Level 3)
  — The Saint-Elsin Foundation (religious organization, Tier 4 board, no labor requests reported)
  — GLMZ Workers' Mutual Network, Sponsorship Division (membership required, free to join)
  — Forward Tier Project (activist-run, explicitly anti-exploitation, significant waitlist)

---

This document may be copied and shared freely. If you need help, ask. That's what this is for.
